current_leader.name: Card authorization integrity-fee prevention engine
current_leader.state_transition: approved authorization -> capture/reversal absent while merchant fulfillment/cancellation state changes -> scheme reversal/clearing deadline approaches -> recommend REVERSE/CAPTURE/NO ACTION -> reconcile avoided integrity fee
current_leader.why_survived: Fresh processor documentation reinforces that authorization expiry alone is not equivalent to timely scheme compliance. Chase states Mastercard card-not-present unused authorizations should be reversed within 72 hours, while Stripe documents uncaptured PaymentIntents being canceled after a default period of 7 days and Adyen commonly expires major-network authorizations after 28 days. This leaves a plausible merchant-state-driven early-reversal gap. At the same time, TD explicitly closes batches after 48 hours where possible to avoid Mastercard's new 72-hour authorization-validity fee, showing that simple batch-timing optimization is already being absorbed first-party. No dominant exact product was found for fulfillment-aware cancellation/reversal before the applicable integrity deadline.
current_leader.strongest_evidence: Chase merchant documentation says Mastercard Processing Integrity applies when an authorization is not used or reversed to Mastercard standards and says card-not-present merchants should reverse within 72 hours. Stripe documents uncaptured PaymentIntents canceling after a default 7-day period, and Adyen commonly expires major-network authorizations after 28 days. TD says it attempts to close batches after 48 hours to avoid Mastercard's 0.0339% authorization-validity fee that applies to transactions cleared after 72 hours. Visa misuse-of-authorization remains $0.15 per non-compliant US transaction; Mastercard integrity fees remain materially higher for some authorization classes.
current_leader.closest_threat: Tagada's cross-processor authorization-window automation remains the closest product threat. Stripe automatic-delayed capture, Shopify capture-at-fulfillment, Adyen capture/cancel APIs, processor batch-closing controls, and scheme-fee intelligence products can absorb parts of the workflow. The remaining whitespace is specifically merchant fulfillment/cancellation state -> early reversal recommendation before scheme penalty, without owning checkout or routing.
current_leader.smallest_intervention: Read authorization, capture and cancellation webhooks plus merchant order/fulfillment status; maintain network/MCC/region deadline rules; alert REVERSE NOW, CAPTURE NOW or NO ACTION with projected avoided fee and evidence. Merchant confirms any write action.
current_leader.monetization: Per verified prevented-fee event or a capped percentage of reconciled scheme-fee savings; only charge a recurring monitoring fee where observed exposure supports it.
current_leader.biggest_unresolved_risk: The incidence denominator remains missing: published fee rates prove loss severity but not how many merchants incur enough stale-authorisation penalties to support a scalable performance-fee business. Some processors may also send network reversals earlier than their user-visible PaymentIntent/authorization expiry state suggests.
current_leader.next_research_test: Find processor/acquirer statement datasets, merchant audits or network/acquirer statistics that reveal integrity/misuse fee count and dollars per 100,000 authorizations by vertical. Separately verify whether major PSPs send network reversal messages before user-visible expiry/cancellation. If incidence is low or PSPs already send timely reversals, demote or reject.

rejections.fatal_flaw: Processor-native automation already attacks the micro-event directly: TD states it closes batches after 48 hours where possible to prevent Mastercard's new 72-hour authorization-validity fee. This is too close to a first-party operational control to support an independent wedge.

Refund/expiry rights are fragmented by product and often self-service or non-refundable. Alibaba Cloud documents multiple resource-plan refund paths and expiry rules directly; other API credit products either make credits non-refundable or non-expiring. The resulting wedge is heterogeneous, overlaps previously rejected broad entitlement monitoring, and is weak against simple self-service reminders.

new_search_rules: Do not equate PSP authorization expiry with scheme-compliant reversal; verify the actual network reversal message timing.
When a processor explicitly auto-adjusts batch timing to avoid a network fee, treat that micro-wedge as first-party absorbed even if other processors do not.
For prepaid-credit opportunities, require a broadly repeatable machine-readable refund right; heterogeneous provider refund policies are not enough.
